checkpoints: A `findOne` followed by a separate `insert` costs two network round-trips to the relational database for every single message, and since this dedup check runs on every send, it puts the database on the hot path for the system's highest-frequency operation.

`findOne` and `insert` are two independent commands rather than one atomic operation, so there is a check-then-act (TOCTOU) window between them: two workers can each run `findOne`, each see no existing row, and both proceed to `insert` and call `send`, producing a duplicate delivery even though the code appears to guard against it.

A unique constraint on `messageId` only converts the race into a database error on the second `insert` after the fact — it does not stop the second worker from having already called `send()` before that insert fails, so it detects the duplicate rather than preventing it.

The fix is to stop treating deduplication as a database read-then-write and instead perform it as a single atomic Redis command, `SET dedup:{messageId} 1 NX EX <ttl>`: because the existence-check and the write happen inside one atomic operation, there is no window in which two concurrent workers can both observe the key as absent.

The `NX` flag makes the `SET` succeed only if the key does not already exist, so the command itself returns success (`"OK"`) to exactly one caller when multiple workers race on the same `messageId`, and every other caller receives `null` and skips sending.

This is a single round-trip and an O(1) key lookup, compared to the original approach's two round-trips against an indexed table, which is what removes the database from the per-message hot path at peak throughput.

The `EX` option attaches a self-expiring TTL to the dedup key, so the dedup store does not grow without bound the way a permanent `sent_messages` table would, since old entries fall out of Redis automatically once the TTL elapses.

Correctness of the fix should be verified by firing the same `messageId` concurrently from multiple workers and asserting that exactly one of them acquires the key and sends, and by comparing round-trip count and latency under load against the original SELECT-then-INSERT path to confirm the throughput improvement.

Keying the rate-limit bucket strictly per user×channel (`rl:<recipient>:<channel>`) correctly isolates one recipient's limit from another's, but Redis Cluster maps that single literal key to exactly one hash slot on exactly one shard.

When one recipient goes viral or one channel gets hammered, every request for that pair funnels through the same key, so its EVAL calls saturate one shard while every other shard in the cluster sits idle — the bottleneck is single-key contention, not total Redis capacity.

The fix is to shard the hot key into N sub-buckets (`rl:<recipient>:<channel>:<shard>` for shard in 0..N-1), each sized to `bucketCapacity/N` and `refillAmount/N`, and route each incoming request to one sub-bucket (round-robin, or hashing a request-local id mod N).
Running the same Lua script against just the routed sub-bucket keeps the per-request check O(1) and local, with no cross-shard read needed to decide allow or deny.

Because the N sub-bucket keys naturally land on different hash slots, a viral recipient's load spreads across up to N shards instead of pinning one; when the total remaining is needed (an admin dashboard, a debug endpoint), it is computed by summing the token count across all N sub-buckets.

Splitting one shared bucket into N even slices is a real trade-off, not a free win: a burst that would have fit under the single bucket can now be rejected if it lands unevenly across sub-buckets, trading some burst-smoothing accuracy for horizontal spread across shards.

For genuinely extreme keys — traffic blowing past every sub-bucket instantly — a cheap in-memory approximate counter at the edge can reject obviously-over-limit requests before they ever issue a Redis EVAL, so Redis only sees traffic with a real chance of being allowed.
Moving the rate-limit Redis onto its own instance, separate from the queue Redis used for job dequeue, prevents a hot rate-limit shard from also starving unrelated queue traffic.

The sharding change should be validated with a load test that drives one hot key alone, measuring per-key p99 latency before and after sharding, and confirming the summed aggregate across the N sub-buckets still enforces the original limit.

When a producer packs every requested channel into the data of a single queue job, the broker only has one pass/fail outcome to react to — it cannot tell that push already succeeded and only email needs another try.

A for-loop that awaits push, then email, then sms inside one processor function has no isolation between channels: an exception thrown while sending email propagates out of the processor and is treated as a failure of the entire job, not just the email step.

Because the retry unit in a job queue is the job itself, retrying that failed job re-runs the processor from the top — so push, which already sent successfully, fires again and reaches the user as a duplicate notification.

The mismatch driving this bug is that the desired unit of retry is one channel, while the actual unit of retry the queue provides is one job; bundling multiple channels into a single job collapses that distinction.

The structural fix is fan-out at the producer: instead of enqueuing one job whose data holds an array of channels, enqueue one separate job per channel (for example via a bulk-add call), using the channel as the job name and giving each job only that channel's payload.
With one job per channel, a failure in the email job causes the broker to retry only that job; the push and sms jobs already completed independently and are left untouched, so they cannot be re-sent.

Wrapping each provider call in a try/catch that swallows the error is not a valid fix, because it prevents the failure from ever surfacing to the queue — the email job is never marked failed, so it is never retried, and the notification is silently lost instead of duplicated.

A meaningful way to verify the fix is to enqueue a multi-channel request where the email provider fails on its first attempt, then confirm push and sms were each delivered exactly once while only the email job shows a retry that eventually succeeds.

Keeping a rate limiter's remaining-token count on a private field of a service instance means every replica running behind a load balancer holds its own independent copy of that count, so the aggregate throughput allowed across all replicas is roughly N times the intended per-key limit.

In-memory counter state does not survive a process restart: a redeploy or crash-restart re-initializes the field to its starting capacity, silently resetting the limiter to full even though no time-based refill was actually earned.

Implementing a Redis-backed limiter as a plain `GET` followed by a plain `SET` is not atomic — the two calls are separate network round trips, so two concurrent requests can both read the same stored token count, both compute the same decremented value, and both write it back, losing one decrement and letting more requests through than the limit allows (a TOCTOU race).

The fix is to collapse the entire read-refill-decrement-write sequence into a single Lua script executed via Redis `EVAL`, because Redis runs each Lua script to completion on its single command thread, so no other client's command can interleave in the middle of the sequence.

The bucket must be keyed per logical entity being limited (for example `user:channel`) so that every replica reads and writes the same shared counter in Redis instead of each maintaining its own state, and the key should carry a TTL/expiry so an idle bucket is cleaned up automatically instead of accumulating in Redis forever.

Overshooting a provider's send-rate limit is a production-severity blocker rather than a style nitpick, because the sending IP or account can get throttled or blocked by the notification provider/carrier, taking down message delivery for the whole system.

This class of bug passes cleanly in a single-instance local or test environment because there is only one process and no real concurrent network round trip to expose the race — it only manifests once the service is actually scaled out to multiple replicas under concurrent load.

Verifying the fix requires a concurrency test: fire capacity-plus-one requests at the same key simultaneously (ideally from at least two separate instances or connections) and assert that exactly one request is rejected, which proves the counting is atomic and shared rather than racy or per-process.

A catch block that simply rethrows an error so the queue's built-in attempts and exponential backoff retry the job is not the same as failover: it re-invokes the exact same primary provider after each backoff delay, so if the primary is genuinely down, every retry hits the same dead endpoint again and the recipient waits through several seconds of dead time for nothing.

Genuine failover switches to a fallback provider within the same attempt — catching the primary's failure and immediately calling the fallback before the job handler returns — rather than letting the error escape to the queue and waiting on a scheduled retry; only when both the primary and the fallback fail should the error propagate to the broker for an actual job-level retry.

On an at-least-once queue, a message can be redelivered because a worker crashes right before the implicit acknowledgment, or because an earlier attempt is retried, and a processor with no idempotency check will send that message again — for a login OTP email that is a user-facing double-send bug, not a cosmetic detail.

Deduplication needs a stable message identifier, supplied by the caller or generated once at the producer, namespaced per delivery channel (for example combining a base message id with the channel name), so the same logical send across retries or channels can be recognized as one intent to deliver rather than several.

Before dispatching, the processor should atomically acquire the message id as a key in a shared store — such as a Redis SET with NX and an expiry — and proceed with sending only if that acquisition succeeds; if the key already exists, the send is skipped because delivery has already happened or is already in flight.

A senior-level PR review separates true blockers — a delivery path that can silently double-send, and a fallback provider that is wired into the constructor but never actually invoked — from nitpicks, and asks about the author's intent, such as whether retrying only the primary was a deliberate interim choice or simply unfinished work, instead of just declaring the code wrong.

Verifying the fix requires two specific tests: one that forces the primary provider to fail and asserts the fallback delivers the message within the same attempt with no multi-second wait, and one that redelivers the same message id twice and asserts the underlying provider's send is invoked exactly once.
